newsitem.title: MOLDOVA: World bank says encouraged by Moldovan reforms.
newsitem.headline: World bank says encouraged by Moldovan reforms.

text.p: The World Bank is encouraged by the reformist stance of Moldova's new government and hopes Chisinau will push on with promised structural reforms, an official said on Wednesday.

"We are very encouraged by the pro-reform declarations of the new Moldovan president and prime minister. We hope their intention to accelerate reforms will be translated into specific actions," James Parks, the Bank's resident representative in Moldova, told a news conference.
The Bank has approved a total $231 million of loans for seven projects to support private sector, structural reforms, export promotion and the development of the agricultural and energy sectors.
A three-year programme ending in 1998 provides for up to $100 million annual disbursments for the agricultural country of 4.3 million people between Ukraine and Romania.
A World Bank mission comes to Moldova in early February to discuss a new $60 million structural adjustment loan.
"We hope 1997 will be the first year when the Bank will invest significant amounts of money in Moldova," Parks said.
He put Moldova in the top rank of former Soviet countries in terms of macroeconomic stabilization, but said it was well behind the Baltic states in terms of structural reforms.
"Countries like Armenia, Georgia, Ukraine, which started reforms later than Moldova, have been catching up in the last years," Parks said.
Moldova brought annual inflation down to 15.1 percent in 1996, keeping the currency stable and increasing external reserves to $315 million.
But structural reforms slowed, contributing to an eight percent GDP decline in 1996 and the build-up of payment arrears.
The aims of the new loan include boosting privatisation, strengthening the framework for public spending and reforming the social safety net and the pension system.
